deep.reconstruction:
The page contains no mathematics: no formulas, derivations or computations. It is a passage of Riemann's natural-philosophical speculation on the physical preconditions of the 'life process' (Lebensprocess). It continues the question at the end of p. 30: why are the four organic elements (C, H, N, O) the universal carriers of the life process?

(a) The reason may lie in properties that distinguish these four elements from all others.
- Property 1: they and their compounds are the hardest of all substances to condense, and some cannot be condensed at all as of the time of writing. This refers to the 'permanent gases' H2, N2 and O2, and also CO, CH4 and NO, none of which had been liquefied before 1877.
- Property 2: the great variety of their compounds and the ease with which these decompose. Riemann himself notes that this could be a consequence rather than a cause of their use in life processes.

(b) He argues that property 1 (difficult condensability) is what makes them suited to life. This follows partly from the factual conditions of the life process listed earlier under 2) and 3), which are not on this page. It follows even more if one traces the phenomena of condensing gases into liquids and solids back to their causes. He announces a hypothesis; at that point the copy notes a gap, apparently a crossed-out passage.

(c) The qualitative force scheme. To explain the relative motions of chemical atoms (simple or compound), one distinguishes approaching causes from separating causes.
- Approaching causes: (1) external forces, i.e. pressure; (2) cohesion and adhesion, jointly called capillary forces.
- Separating causes: (1) thermal repulsion; (2) chemical repulsion.

The states of aggregation are then characterised by which forces balance which:
- Gaseous state: thermal repulsion alone, without help from chemical repulsion, balances the external pressure. In modern terms, this is the ideal-gas regime, p = nRT/V (my gloss).
- Chemical repulsion shows itself only subordinately in gases, in the mixing of gases (diffusion).
- Capillary forces show themselves only subordinately in gases, in their condensation near the boundary of solids and liquids. This is adsorption (my gloss).
- The liquid state is continued on p. 32: there thermal repulsion balances external pressure only with the help of chemical repulsion. Capillary forces alone, without external pressure, cannot balance the repulsive forces, and they appear as capillary phenomena.

The scheme is a qualitative molecular-force picture of the states of matter, loosely anticipating the attraction/repulsion split of van der Waals (1873). No quantitative law is stated. The handwriting and the editorial bracket '((Lücke, durchgestrichen))' suggest this is a later fair copy, not an autograph.
errors: Factual overstatement: 'they and their compounds are the hardest of all substances to condense' is false for carbon itself, which is an extremely refractory solid. It also fails for many of their compounds, such as water, CO2 (liquefied by Faraday in 1823) and NH3. The claim fits only H2, N2, O2 and a few compounds (CO, CH4, NO) that were 'permanent gases' before 1877.

The force classification is qualitative and is not justified on this page. 'Chemical repulsion' as a separate cause has no clear modern counterpart: diffusion in gas mixtures is not due to repulsion. Its later role in stabilising liquids is likewise not a recognised mechanism.
The appeal to 'conditions 2) and 3)' refers to an earlier list that is not on this page or on p. 30 as given, so the argument cannot be checked here.

results.what: Hypothesis that the organogenic elements C, H, N, O are suited to life because they and their compounds are hard to condense

Qualitative classification of interatomic causes: attractive (external pressure, capillary/cohesion-adhesion forces) vs repulsive (thermal, chemical). States of aggregation characterised by which forces balance external pressure.
results.modern_name: qualitative molecular-force theory of states of matter (cf. Laplace capillarity, kinetic theory, van der Waals attraction/repulsion picture)
results.usually_credited_to: Laplace/Young (capillary forces, c. 1805); Clausius/Krönig (kinetic gas theory, 1856-57); van der Waals (1873)

deep.surprise_reason: This is purely qualitative speculation consistent with Riemann's known natural-philosophy fragments: Gravitation und Licht, and the Naturphilosophie pieces printed in the Werke. It contains no mathematics or novel quantitative result. The force scheme is commonplace mid-19th-century physics.

checkable.asserts: Modern gloss, not in the text: in the gaseous state the 'thermal repulsion' (kinetic pressure nRT/V) alone balances the external pressure p.
Modern gloss, not in the text: van der Waals equation, where the cohesion term a*n**2/V**2 plays the role of Riemann's attractive 'capillary forces' that become important on condensation.

transcription_corrections: The transcription of this page agrees well with the image. The marginal pencil note read as 'bis Seite[?] 13[?]' is plausible but uncertain; it may be a reference such as 'bis Seite 13'.
The pencil mark read as '#7' looks like two crossed strokes followed by '7'; it is an archival or numbering mark, not text.
The page appears to be a later fair copy (editorial bracket '((Lücke, durchgestrichen))'), not Riemann's autograph.

Next page (p. 32), line 1: 'ist die chemische Repulsion nur mit Hülfe der chemischen' is contradictory. Given the parallel with the gas sentence here, it should almost certainly read 'ist die thermische Repulsion nur mit Hülfe der chemischen'.
